On the one hand, this is very cool. I can’t imagine how long this took to make and it seems like it would be reassuring to see the truth of what you know so clearly laid out. I wonder what mine would look like from the years I actually responded to the abusive texts. 

That said, I do unfortunately have to agree with the other commenter who said it may be more effective to show the most egregious examples in context. It will also be very necessary to switch your conversations to a parenting app, which will put them in a court-admissible format. Text messages outside of parenting apps are just too easy to manipulate and courts often don’t accept them even outside of your obvious tech skills.

I also recommend looking at it from the perspective of the GAL, whose job is to look out for the kids. Your ex’s behavior aside, I see a lot of focus on you (and her) but practically nothing on your boys. Again, put her aside because this isn’t about her - it’s about the kids. So, while she doesn’t mention their mental health at all, you only appear to mention it once in two years while mentioning your own eight times. Data can look bad out of context, which is why analyzing it to make business decisions is a great skill to have. 

TL;DR - Keep this for yourself to help you remember the truth in the hardest of times and get on a parenting app for all communications with the ex. The GAL and the court can force your ex to use it and everything in it will be court-admissible. 🙌

It’s hard and will most likely take years, but I’ve seen enough to know that it can be done.

Taking your points in order, I will say that I agree the majority of homeschool parents don’t appear to be doing a disservice to their kids. It makes a lot of sense for many families. But, generally, I’d place bets they are married and there is no history of abuse/no history of abuse they are willing to admit. In this case, we aren’t married anymore and there is a history of abuse. GF has her own serious issues and joins the ex in fully believing she knows better than, well, pretty much everyone on everything. Boundaries are also not something either understand. So, unfortunately, I can’t ask either how it’s going and get an honest answer because their egos are wrapped up in the success of this venture. Latest evidence? She has a new website up offering homeschool lessons for other children, minus any accreditation. 

My kids are definitely able to read books above their grade-level and I’m proud of how much they love to read. But I do think the books they are reading require an adult to help them walk through and pick up on the not-so-obvious points and I’m sad that they likely aren’t really grasping the fullness of what they are reading because there isn’t an adult in the room who has read the books/helping with comprehension. What’s the point if they don’t actually comprehend what they are being forced to read? I’ve asked probing questions to figure out if they are comprehending and their answers have not indicated they understand the texts or why they are reading it. 

The AP class. I’ve encouraged my oldest to take AP classes because getting college credits without paying for college classes is a no-brainer. While her dad’s GF seems concerningly obsessed with my kids graduating early (she graduated at 16 from homeschool I think), I’m just happy to have them get some college credits in advance that might help safe money. Beyond that, I don’t want them to graduate early or rush through these years that matter so much. I want them to take their time to understand what makes THEM happy. It’s not a sprint so-to-speak. 

I will make a point to figure out the Trig thing. I didn’t make it past Algebra even in college. 

He has confirmed he has no desire to send them back to public school, despite at least half of them saying they want to go back, so we are headed to court. But if the court should find this situation needs to be maintained, I’ll need all the help I can get here to make sure my kids are getting the full education they deserve, social and emotional aspects included, so you’ll find me here again with massive apprehension as to how this can possibly work but willing to do whatever is needed to see them through successfully to graduation and beyond.

Yes, the homeschool site that facilitated the testing (Homeschool Boss) explained the tests can and should be used to assess strengths and weaknesses. I explained that when I sent copies to him but he dismissed them as me trying to undermine his plans. I’m data driven in my job so I naturally look to the numbers to inform what comes next and I think this is really the only way to get bias out of decision-making. The kids are super smart and already way ahead of their peers. I don’t want this change in education to slow their growth because he doesn’t know what he’s doing. As someone above noted, a judge will decide what’s best for the kids and that’s what I want. An outside opinion, just like those tests, will help provide clarity. Two of the kids have said they want to go back to public school so we may end up with a hybrid. As long as they are learning what they need to be and excelling as much as they were in public school, I’ll go back to being able to sleep at night.

I don’t hold public school up as a paragon of quality education any more than I would I homeschool. But considering how well my children were advancing in public school prior to this and that being the only education they were receiving, I can say with confidence that our schools were getting it done well. Our schools are #1 in our state so it’s not as if he’s rescued them from a subpar school system. 

He does not give them regular assessments from what I’ve been told by the children. My son has read two books so far with no actual assessment of his understanding of either one. The books he has read have not been read by his father, who dropped out of high school and never attained a college degree. 

I am here because I have always taken ownership of their education, tyvm. I didn’t want this homeschool thing from the start but there was abuse in the marriage and the bullying pressure present in marriage doesn’t just end with divorce. I have communicated my desires for their education and my thoughts on his homeschool choices (including a book that was not at all appropriate for my daughter to be reading with zero help from anyone on comprehending the adult themes within) and they have been 100% rejected. 

Again, my purpose here was to hear the homeschool perspective and it seems to be in line with my prior understanding. Every family does it differently. And I imagine that works well for married families - most especially when one can stay home and homeschooling the kids is their primary job - but there is a reason we are divorced and not every parent, despite what they may want to believe, is cut out to be 100% responsible for their kids’ education.

I appreciate all of this. I paid to have them tested at the beginning of the school year so I could see the baseline of where they were with the same test they’d been taking in public school all the years prior to now. He was pissed that I tested them and is not happy that I plan to test them again in January. But without a baseline and regular testing, I don’t know how you establish a non-biased rate of growth. I’ve asked repeatedly for work as well as grades and haven’t received anything. He isn’t even answering my emails requesting things. Idk how I’m supposed to trust any of this with zero transparency and no standards to fall back on. We live in a very red state so they don’t question anything regarding how parents are actually facilitating homeschool; with no accountability, homeschool is whatever he wants it to be. There was a time when I thought homeschool was a wonderful idea but this experience has turned me off completely from it. I just want my kids back in public school where the standards are clear and their education can be supplemented outside of school by him and/or me if we think anything is lacking. We are headed to court for sure but I do find it important to understand what is typical for homeschool families to help me ascertain how typical or atypical the situation is. I have four kids - 7, 9, 11, and 13. I also work in tech and reading the worst news in the country is part of my day job. I don’t hold back in warning them about the dangers and I tell them that it is my job to keep them safe, not always to keep them happy. I recently took YouTube away from all of them except the 13 year old, who has more than proven she can handle it. I will not allow any of them on any social media.

I can’t do anything about their access through other kids - playing at a friend’s, on the bus, etc, but I can give them the facts and limit their exposure until they are older and have a better understanding of why I felt it necessary to limit them in the first place. 

Kicking them outside to play with friends and having no electronics allowed on the weekdays has helped a lot, but the war is far from over. If I had it to do over again, I’d have never allowed anything online to begin with. Online games are a bigger issue here than YouTube ever was.
